t.1.141.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: But Bhīmasena, seeing that rākṣasa, spoke these angry words concerning his sister, as though laughing.
t.1.141.2: What use to you, Hiḍimbā, are these who sleep peacefully, once they are woken? Come at me swiftly, you evil-minded man-eater!
t.1.141.4: This girl does not desire me here today of her own will, for she is driven by the bodiless god of love who moves within the body. She is your sister, O evil-minded one, O destroyer of the rākṣasas' fame!
t.1.141.3: Come, strike at me alone; you ought not to kill a woman, especially when she has done no wrong and the wrong has been done by another.
t.1.141.7: Come and fight with me, one against one, O man-eater! I alone shall lead you today to the abode of Yama.
t.1.141.6: Since the fault was committed by Anaṅga, you, O Rākṣasa, should not kill her here; while I stand by, O evil-souled one, you ought not to slay a woman.
t.1.141.5: It was at your command that she came here, and having seen my form, the timid one now desires me; she does not disgrace the family.
t.1.141.9: Today let the flesh-eaters, hawks and jackals, rejoicing, drag about on the ground the limbs of you, slain by me in battle.
t.1.141.8: Today, O Rākṣasa, let your head, crushed by the flat of my hand, be split apart, crushed as though under the foot of a mighty elephant.
t.1.141.10: In a moment today I shall make this forest free of thorns, this forest which was ever defiled before by you as you devoured men.
t.1.141.11: Today, O wicked one, my sister will see you, huge as a mountain, dragged by me along the ground, like a great elephant dragged by a lion.
t.1.141.12: When you have been slain by me, O disgrace of the Rākṣasas, the men who roam the forest will wander through this forest free from harm.
t.1.141.13: What use to you is this vain roaring and boasting, O man? Accomplish all this in deed first, and then you may boast; do not delay.
t.1.141.15: I shall not harm these ones for now; let them sleep as they please. It is you alone, O evil-minded one, speaker of unpleasant words, whom I strike down today!
t.1.141.16: Having drunk your blood from your limbs, I shall then afterwards kill these men too, and after that this woman who has done what displeases me.
t.1.141.14: And as for your thinking yourself mighty, though you are without prowess, today, once you have met with me, you will find out how superior in strength you really are.
t.1.141.17: Having spoken thus, the man-eater, enraged, raised his arm and rushed at Bhīmasena, the tamer of foes.
t.1.141.18: As he swiftly rushed upon him, Bhīma of terrible prowess, as if laughing, seized the arm he had forcefully struck out.
t.1.141.19: Seizing him by force as he struggled, Bhīma dragged him eight bow-lengths away from that place, as a lion drags a small animal.
t.1.141.20: Then that rākṣasa, enraged at being dragged away by force by the Pāṇḍava, clasped Bhīmasena in his arms and let out a terrifying roar.
t.1.141.21: Again the mighty Bhīma dragged him away by force, thinking, "Let there be no noise to disturb my brothers, who are sleeping peacefully."
t.1.141.22: Having closed with one another, the two dragged each other about with great force; the Rākṣasa and Bhīmasena displayed the utmost prowess.
t.1.141.23: Then the two of them broke great trees and dragged up creepers, like a pair of furious sixty-year-old elephants in rut.
t.1.141.24: Awakened by the great noise of those two, those bulls among men, together with their mother, saw Hiḍimbā standing before them.
